The aim of this study was to reveal the success of allergen immunotherapy (AIT) in Landspitali from 1977-2006. MATERIAL AND METHODS: During the study period a total number of 289 individuals underwent immunotherapy in outpatient clinic of allergy and asthma in Landspítali. A total number of 169 individuals were contacted, of whom 128 (76%) accepted to participate in the study. The evaluation was based on medical records, standardized questionnaire and skin-prick tests. RESULTS: Patients were evaluated on the average of 20 years after finishing treatment. 118 (92%) patients were desensitized to grass pollen, to birch pollen (30%), cat dander (30%) and dust mite (28%). At the time of the study 67% reported to be asymptomatic or with greatly improved allergy symptoms. Males had better response to AIT than women (p=0.04). Participants with positive family history of allergy and/or asthma in first degree relatives also reported better response to AIT (p=0.02). Furthermore, AIT to grass pollen and dust mite seemed to be more effective than AIT to cat dander and birch (p=0.04). AIT was also shown to reduce asthma. CONCLUSION: AIT for 3-5 years provides significant beneficial effect of allergy and asthma symptoms in patients who undergo such therapy. Finally, it s findings support the notion that AIT may reduce the risk of new allergic manifestations.
Local and Systemic IgE in the Evaluation and Treatment of Allergy; Traditional descriptions of type I hypersensitivity and its manifestations center on systemic immunoglobulin E (IgE)-mediated reactions to inciting antigens. Hence, many current diagnostic and therapeutic measures are based on systemic skin testing for allergy, systemic pharmacotherapy, and immunotherapy. Recent developments in rhinology and pulmonology, particularly in defining the phenomenon of local IgE production in various airway inflammatory conditions, have an impact on both medical and surgical diagnosis and management of these conditions. This review includes a discussion of allergy as a systemic disease, current systemic diagnostic and management strategies for allergy, and local IgE presence and synthesis in the upper and lower airways. © 2010 Elsevier Inc.
The biological potency of different extracts for sublingual immunotherapy assessed by skin prick tests; The standardization of allergen extracts is of primary relevance to the clinical efficacy. Biological standardization procedures are widely used in the commercial production of vaccines. We tested, in grass-allergic patients, the potency of three different grass extracts for sublingual immunotherapy by means of skin prick tests. Specific IgE against Phl p 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 11 and 12 were also assayed. Allerslit® and Sublivac® were directly applied as skin test. Grazax®, was prepared by dissolving two tablets in 2mL saline. Thirty-three subjects (mean age 38.8) were studied. The skin response was significantly different among extracts, decreasing from Allerslit to Grazax (t test <0.01), but all the extract produced a skin response greater than histamine. All the subjects had specific IgE to Phl p 1 and Phl p 4 but 24% did not have specific IgE to Phl p 5. In those subjects the skin response to the three extracts did not differ from that of Phl p 5-positive subjects. Our findings confirm that there is a variability in the biological potency among different extracts. In addition, the standardization of grass extracts based on Phl p 5 only, may be insufficient in some cases.
Subcutaneous immunotherapy with a preparation with optimised allergen aluminium hydroxide ratio: A randomised parallel-group clinical trial investigating safety and tolerability; Background: For subcutaneous immunotherapy (SCIT) allergens usually are adsorbed to aluminium hydroxide (alum) for slow allergen release (depot effect). In addition alum also acts as an adjuvant that enhances the immunological effect. Therefore, a SCIT product with an optimised allergen/alum ratio allows for reducing the maximum dose applied for maintenance therapy and shorter up-dosing schedules. In a clinical trial safety and tolerability profile of a product with an optimised allergen/alum ratio has been investigated. Methods: In a randomised, controlled, parallel-group trial patients with rhinoconjunctivitis with/without asthma induced by grass pollen were treated with a SCIT depot preparation (four grasses and rye, AVANZ, ALK-Abello, Hørsholm, Denmark) containing 15% of the allergen content and 50% of the alum content compared with the widely used ALK allergen product for SCIT (Alutard SQ, ALK-Abelló, Hørsholm, Denmark). Therapy was initiated utilising an up-dosing phase with five injections (300, 600, 3000, 6000, 15 000 SQ+) with weekly intervals in group 1 and 3-4 days intervals in group 2 and was continued by two maintenance injections of 15 000 SQ+ with 14 and 28 days intervals. Results: In total 400 patients were treated (group 1: 201, group 2: 199) with the five injection up-dosing schedule. The trial was completed according to the injection schedule by 358 patients (group 1: 185, group 2: 173). Fewer local and systemic reactions were observed during up-dosing with one week intervals (group 1) compared with 3-4 days intervals (group 2). Local reactions were observed in group 1 in 68/201 patients (33.8%) and 93/199 (46.7%) patients in group 2. Delayed systemic reactions (1 h after the injection or later) occurred in 41/201 (20.4%) patients in group 1 and 63/199 (31.7%) patients in group 2 predominantly as rhinoconjunctivits or urticaria. The frequency of local and systemic reactions was much lower for the two maintenance injections in both treatment groups. Conclusion: Using a five injections up-dosing schedule a SCIT product with an optimised allergen/adjuvant ratio (AVANZ) was found to be well tolerated. Fewer local and systemic reactions were observed for up-dosing with injection intervals of 1 week compared with 3-4 days injection intervals.
Effect of birch pollen specific immunotherapy on birch pollen-related hazelnut allergy; Background: Birch pollen allergy can lead to pollen-related hazelnut allergy, due to cross-reactivity via the major allergens in birch (Bet v 1) and hazelnut (Cor a 1). However, it is unclear whether birch pollen specific immunotherapy (SIT) can be used to treat the associated hazelnut allergy. Objective: To evaluate the effect of birch pollen SIT on clinical and immunological parameters of birch pollen and hazelnut allergy. Methods: In a double-blind study, nineteen patients with birch pollen allergy and concomitant hazelnut allergy were randomly assigned to 1 year subcutaneous birch pollen SIT (Alutard SQ, ALK-Abelló) or placebo-treatment (histamine). Reactions upon accidental hazelnut ingestion during the treatment period were recorded in diaries. Eliciting doses for hazelnut and symptoms (visual analogue scale) were determined by double-blind placebo-controlled food challenge (DBPCFC) before and after 1 year of treatment. Titrated skin prick tests were performed using birch pollen and hazelnut extract, Bet v 1 and Cor a 1, before and at various time points after treatment. Grass pollen, house dust mite and cat extract were used as control allergens. IgE, IgG4 and IgG levels in serum were measured for birch pollen and hazelnut extract, Bet v 1 and Cor a 1. In addition, the effect of SIT on IgE-facilitated allergen binding (IgE-FAB) was measured by flow cytometry. Results: Hazelnut eliciting doses and symptoms measured by VAS during DBPCFC did not change upon treatment in the SIT or the placebo group. Reactions upon accidental hazelnut ingestion were less frequently reported in the SIT group. In the SIT group, skin prick test responses to birch pollen, Bet v 1 and Cor a 1, but not to control allergens, decreased significantly upon treatment. Serum levels of IgG4 and IgG towards birch pollen and Bet v 1, and IgG towards Cor a 1, showed a significant increase. IgE-FAB was inhibited to a significantly larger extent for all allergens in the SIT group than in the placebo group. Conclusion: No objective clinical improvement of hazelnut allergy was observed by DBPCFC, though reported reactions upon accidental ingestions were less frequent. Birch pollen SIT induced significant changes in skin prick test, IgG responses and IgE-FAB towards Bet v 1 and the cross-reactive allergen Cor a 1. This indicates that birch pollen SIT may be useful to treat the associated hazelnut allergy, but a higher dose or prolonged treatment may be necessary.
ImmunoCAP ISAC IgE and IgG4 as tools for monitoring specific immunotherapy; Background: Specific immunotherapy (SIT) is an effective treatment of pollen allergy. However, its effect on pollen-related food allergy remains unclear. Specific (s) IgE and IgG4 can be measured during SIT to monitor immunological effect and perhaps to predict treatment efficacy, but its usefulness have been hampered by the lack of component-specific antibody tests. Methods: Sera from eight allergic patients treated with conventional birch (n = 8) and timothy pollen (n = 6) SIT, and three non-treated controls, were analyzed using ImmunoCAP ISAC® IgE and IgG4, novel assays that allows semi-quantitative measurements of IgE and IgG4 antibodies against 103 allergenic components simultaneously. Sera were obtained at start of SIT (baseline), at regular intervals during the upscaling phase, and during the 1st and 2nd birch pollen season (BPS) after start of SIT. Results: All eight SIT-patients had IgE, and 5 had IgG4, to Bet v 1 from birch at baseline. Common was also IgE to Cor a 1.04 (hazelnut) and Mal d 4 (apple) and IgG4 to Api g 1 (celery). Median number of sensitizations to the 11 PR-10 allergens included was 5.5 (range: 2-9). The corresponding figure for sIgG4 was 2 (range: 0-8). The IgE levels to Bet v 1 decreased for 7 SIT-patients at 1st and 2nd BPS (median decrease from baseline: 76%, range: 53%-89%) while IgG4 dramatically increased in all 8 during SIT (median increase: 725%, range: 34%-7450%). In some patients, there was also a small increase in IgG4 to several other PR-10 allergens, often from non detectable levels. Of the 6 patients treated with grass-SIT, IgE to Phl p 1 (n = 5) and Phl p 5 (n = 3) was most common at baseline. Generally, the sIgE levels fell during SIT. Only one grass SIT-patient had IgG4 at baseline to all eight timothy allergens included. The other 5 patients developed new IgG4 reactivities to most timothy components, but mainly to Phl p 5. Only one SIT-patient had IgE to the five profilins included and none had IgE to the two polcalcins (cross-reactive panallergens) at baseline. One had low levels of IgG4 to the profilins and polcalcins at baseline. Three patients developed new sensitizations to profilins. In two of them, IgG4 was developed against the same allergen components. Altogether, three negative SIT-patients developed IgG4 to most profilins and polcalcins and one patient developed IgG4 to all profilins except Phl p 12. Conclusion: ImmunoCAP ISAC IgE and IgG4 offer new possibilities to study detailed serological changes during SIT.
Decreased maturation of human oral mucosal dendritic cells compared to epidermal dendritic cells upon binding of birch and grass pollen allergen; Background: Allergen-specific immunotherapy (AIT) remains the only effective causal treatment for allergic rhinitis. The invasive character of subcutaneous immunotherapy and severe systemic adverse reactions enforced the search for novel, non-invasive applications strategies. In this regard sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) has been shown to be a safe and effective alternative. Further on, recently published data could demonstrate safety and efficacy of epicutaneous application of grass pollen allergen. The induction of allergen-specific regulatory T cells (Tregs) has been postulated as an important immunological mechanism of AIT. Without much doubt, local antigen-presenting cells such oral mucosal dendritic cells (oDCs) or epidermal DCs (eDCs) are critical as they are able to induce Tregs. The current paradigm postulates that in contrast to mature DCs, immature DCs preferentially induce tolerance. However, only little is known about the impact of allergen uptake by oDCs and eDCs on their maturation state. For this reason, resorption of the allergen Bet v1 or Phlp 5 and their impact on the maturation of human oDC as compared to eDCs was studied in an ex vivo model. Methods: Human oral mucosal and epidermal biopsies were placed on petri-dishes and incubated at 4°C and 37°C with PBS containing 100 μg/ml FITC-coupled Phlp 5 or Bet v1. After 1 h of incubation, tissue was washed with PBS and placed in medium at 37°C for DC migration. Maturation state of CD1a+ DCs was analysed after 36 h, measuring CD83 and CCR7 expression. Results: While migration of eDCs from epidermis previously stimulated with Phl p5 led to full maturation of eDCs reflected by induction of CD83 and lymph node homing receptor CCR7 expression, migrated oDCs displayed only reduced expression of maturation marker CD83 and little amounts of CCR7. Most interestingly, oDCs bound to allergen displayed significantly lower expression of CD83 and CCR7 compared to oDCs, which did not bind any allergen. Conclusion: Binding of allergen to eDCs leads to their full maturation, while maturation of oDCs was inhibited, which might have an impact on their tolerogenic properties during AIT.
Application of mass spectrometry to the characterisation and quantification of pharmaceutical-grade allergens; Background: Structural characterization and accurate quantification of major allergens are needed to support the development of high-quality products for specific immunotherapy. Herein, we investigate the pertinence of mass spectrometry (MS) to establish primary structure, monitor structural modifications and obtain quantitative data on major allergens. Methods: Matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight (MALDI-TOF) and high resolution/high mass accuracy electrospray (ESI) MS were combined to determine the primary sequence variations of relevant mite, grass or birch pollen allergens. Purified allergens were analyzed either as intact proteins or following reduction, alkylation and tryptic digestion. Liquid chromatography (LC)-ESI-MS/MS was applied to the detection of species-specific isoforms and quantification of grass pollen group 1 allergens. To this aim 3 target tryptic peptides were monitored in comparison with synthetic peptides labeled with [13C6,15N]Leu and [13C9,15N]Phe used for calibration. Results: In a first MS study, group 1 pollen allergens from five different Pooideae species were shown to exhibit significant intra-and inter-species primary sequence variability. They also displayed variations in proline hydroxylation, N-glycosylation motifs and O-glycosylation. Two MS-assays were consequently developed to monitor a five grass mix vaccine, namely (i) an identity test detecting species-specific group 1-derived peptides, that demonstrated the presence of components from all species in the mix and (ii) an assay for quantifying all the group 1 isoforms, that confirmed batch consistency. In a second study, variants of the house dust mite allergen Der p 2 were characterized in pharmaceutical-grade material, showing the relative contribution of Der p 2.0101, 2.0105, 2.0109 and 2.0110 isoforms. In a third MS study, a recombinant Bet v 1α product intended for a phase III clinical trial was characterized. Primary structure was entirely confirmed as well as low levels of degradation products. Conclusion: MS represents a very suitable approach for in-depth characterization and quantification of pharmaceutical grade relevant allergens intended for specific immunotherapy.

Total medication score was reduced during the study for the active group while it remained unchanged for the placebo group (see Pfaar/Klimek). At baseline mean single symptom scores were comparable between the active and placebo groups. It is an effective treatment for rhinoconjunctivitis.

Response to pollen immunotherapy in local allergic rhinitis; Background: Patients with local allergic rhinitis (LAR) present in situ synthesis of specific-IgE and nasal inflammatory response induced by aeroallergens. The aim of this study was explore the clinical and immunological response to specific immunotherapy (SIT) with grass pollen in these patients. Methods: Twenty adult patients with grass pollen LAR were included in an open observational study. Ten patients were treated with subcutaneous SIT with grass during 6 months and with symptomatic treatment (antihistamine and/or intranasal corticoteroids) and the other ten patients with symptomatic treatment only. Efficacy endpoints comprised response to NAPT-grass, SPT, symptoms and medication scores. Serum and nasal lavage samples were freezed to further studies. Results: In the active group NAPT-grass was negative in three patients after 6 month-SIT, and the others seven needed 50 or 100 times more allergen to achieve a positive response. SPT became positive to grass in four patients after 6 month. Symptoms and medication scores showed important decreases in the next spring (70% and 80% respectively). No adverse effects were detected. In the control group no differences were found in NAPT-grass, SPT, symptom and medication scores. Conclusions: Treatment with SIT with grass induced increase of tolerance to the aeroallergen, reduction of symptoms and rescue medication in LAR patients. Conversion from negative to positive SPT may indicate that LAR can be a first step in the natural evolution toward allergic rhinitis. Follow-up and double-blind pacebo-controlled studies are needed to prove the efficacy and safety of SIT in subject with LAR.

Optimised allergen: Adjuvant ratio potentiates immunogenicity of AlOH-formulated Phleum pratense extract; Background: Specific immunotherapy (SIT) administered either subcutaneously (SCIT) or sublingually in the form of Allergy Immunotherapy Tablets (AIT) have proven sustained clinical efficacy against grass-pollen induced allergic rhinoconjunctivitis. While grass AIT can be initiated directly with the recommended maintenance dose of allergen, gradual updosing over a period of weeks is the recommended regimen for SCIT. Commonly, in commercial products for SCIT the specific allergen is formulated with an adjuvant, most often in the form of aluminium hydroxide (AlOH). The mechanism behind the therapeutic effect of SIT is not completely known. However, it has been shown that allergen-specific IgG antibodies are induced after successful SIT. Here we investigate the possibility of optimising the formulation of AlOH-based grass-pollen allergy vaccines for SCIT in a way that allows for shorter updosing regimens while maintaining the immunogenicity of the vaccine. Methods: Mice were immunised every second week with a conventionally formulated vaccine containing a maintenance dose of 20 kSQ Phl p extract adsorbed to 0.228 mg AlOH, a diluted maintenance dose of 3 kSQ Phl p extract adsorbed to 0.034 mg AlOH or an alternative formulation that consisted of 3 kSQ Phl p extract in the maintenance dose adsorbed to 0.114 mg AlOH. Kinetics of Phl p specific IgG1 antibody responses in serum were quantified. Allergenicity, measured as the ability of the formulations to activate human basophils, was also determined. Results: There were no differences in Phl p-specific IgG1 antibody responses between the groups immunised with either 20 kSQ Phl p + 0.228 mg AlOH or 3 kSQ Phl p + 0.114 mg AlOH. However, immunisation with the new alternative formulation with 3 kSQ Phl p extract + 0.114 mg gave rise to significantly higher IgG1 antibody responses as compared to the group immunised with 3 kSQ Phl p extract + 0.034 mg AlOH. The allergenicity of the 3 kSQ Phl p + 0.114 mg AlOH formulation was 5-20 fold reduced as compared to the 20 kSQ Phl p + 0.228 mg AlOH formulation. Conclusions: The optimisation of the ratio between allergen and adjuvant allows for administration of a lower dose of allergen while maintaining the immunogenicity of the product and at the same time reducing the allergenicity. This study indicates that the optimisation of the ratio between the allergen and the adjuvant could benefit the safety/efficacy profile and allow for shorter updosing.
Recombinant hypoallergenic variants of Phl p 5: Candidates for allergen-specific immunotherapy; Background: Group 5 allergens are major allergens of grasses. Together with group 1 allergens they account for the majority of IgE-reactivity in sera of grass pollen-allergic subjects. Recombinant Timothy grass (Phleum pratense) Phl p 5a and Phl p 5b have already been used in clinical trials of allergen-specific immunotherapy as part of a cocktail of natively folded recombinant allergens. The development of hypoallergenic allergens should further improve allergen-specific immunotherapy by reducing the risk of anaphylactic reactions at increased therapeutic dosage. Methods: A set of variants of Phl p 5 with mutations at proline sites were constructed and expressed in E. coli. The purified proteins were compared with physicochemical methods such as SDS-PAGE, UV/vis-spectroscopy, size-exclusion chromatography and multiple angle light-scattering, as well as immunological methods such as IgE-binding assays, basophil activation tests and T-cell stimulation assays. Results: The mutation of proline residues preferably located in loops connecting adjacent α-helices resulted in molecules with decreased IgE-binding. A strong reduction of IgE-binding could be achieved by combining multiple proline mutations. However, some proline residues were found to be crucial for maintaining solubility or homogeneity of those variants. Deletion of P211 always resulted in aggregation, whereas substitution of P211 with leucine yielded soluble hypoallergenic molecules. Maintaining the prolines P146 and P155 yielded pure monomeric preparations, whereas deletion of these residues resulted in a mixture of monomers and dimers. Selected candidates with excellent physicochemical characteristics proved to be both hypoallergenic and T-cell reactive. Conclusion: The hypoallergenic Phl p 5 variant with deletions of prolines at position 57, 58, 117, 180 and 229 and a substitution of proline 211 with leucine is an excellent candidate for allergen-specific immunotherapy. This variant can be produced with high yield in E. coli and the purified protein meets the high demands made for recombinant therapeutics.
Recombinant hypoallergenic variants of Phl p 6: Candidates for allergen-specific immunotherapy; Background: Phl p 6 is a major allergen of Timothy grass (Phleum pratense). Group 6 allergens have been found only in Timothy and Kentucky blue grass so far. However, despite the observed structural similarity of Phl p 6 and the Phl p 5 N-terminus, immunological differences resulting from unique Phl p 6 epitopes can be observed. Therefore recombinant Phl p 6 has been used in clinical trials of allergen-specific immunotherapy as part of a cocktail of recombinant allergens with native fold. Hypoallergenic variants are believed to further improve allergen-specific immunotherapy. Methods: A set of variants of Phl p 6 with mutations at proline sites were constructed and expressed in E. coli. The purified proteins were compared with physicochemical methods such as SDS-PAGE, UV/vis-spectroscopy, size-exclusion chromatography and multiple angle light-scattering, as well as immunological methods such as IgE-binding assays, basophil activation tests and T-cell stimulation assays. Results: The mutation of proline residues preferably located in loops connecting adjacent α-helices resulted in molecules with decreased IgE-binding. Deletion of proline 29 and 30 proved to have the strongest effect on IgE-reactivity, whereas the mutation of proline 101 had almost no effect. A further reduction of IgE-binding could be obtained by combining multiple proline mutations. Combining deletions of P29 and P30 with mutations of P57 and/or P79 showed a strong hypoallergenic effect. Combination mutants that carry a modification of P57 were found to consist of a mixture of monomers and dimers. In contrast those mutations that maintain P57 and have mutations at P79 are monomeric molecules with excellent physicochemical and hypoallergenic characteristics. Conclusion: A hypoallergenic Phl p 6 variant with mutations of prolines at position 29, 30 and 79 is an excellent candidate for allergen-specific immunotherapy. This variant can be produced with high yield in E. coli and the purified protein meets the high demands made for recombinant therapeutics.

Efficacy and safety of grass monomeric allergoid sublingual immunotherapy: A randomised study comparing two different treatment regimens versus drug therapy alone; Background: Monomeric allergoid sublingual immunotherapy (allergoid SLIT) proved to be well tolerated, safe and effective in patients with respiratory allergy. A drawback is that the achievement of a clinical benefit using a standard regimen requires a long time before efficacy may be appreciated. Aim of this study was to investigate whether different regimens of allergoid SLIT (i.e. perennial versus preseasonal) may affect the clinical outcome. Methods: Thirty-three adult patients (mean age 29 ± 10.1 years, 13 F) with allergic rhinoconjunctivitis with/without mild intermittent asthma were enrolled into the study and randomised to receive either allergoid SLIT with a perennial regimen (group 1: 10 patients, 1000 AU/week for 2 years, for a total amount of 100 000 UA) or allergoid SLIT with a pre-seasonal regimen (group 2: 11 patients, 5000 AU/week for 10 weeks/year for 2 years, for a total amount of 104 000 UA) or drug therapy alone (group 3: 11 patients). At baseline and at the end of the second pollen season a Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) was performed to assess the patients' well-being. Symptom score (sneezing, rhinorrea, nasal congestion, ocular symptoms, cough, asthma symptoms) and drug consumption (antihistamines, broncodilators, nasal, bronchial and oral corticosteroids) were also evaluated with monthly diary cards. Comparison of efficacy of conventional subcutaneous immunotherapy and ultra-short subcutaneous immunotherapy containing monophosphoryl lipid a (MPL): Results of a multicentre observational study after 2 years of treatment; Background: Greater understanding of the disease process in allergic conditions has allowed the development of specific immunotherapies which target the underlying pathology. Data after 1 year of treatment were presented previously. Methods: Total of 215 patients (78 with grass and 137 with tree pollen-related rhinoconjunctivitis and/or asthma) were enrolled. Lack of association between clinical efficacy and cellular immune responses in the blood during grass pollen sublingual immunotherapy; Background: The efficacy of a 300-IR 5-grass-pollen SLIT tablet on rhinoconjonctivitis symptoms was confirmed in a double blind, placebo controlled study conducted in an allergen challenge chamber (ACC). We took advantage of this study to inquire whether changes in basophil activation and T cell responses can be used as biomarkers predicting efficacy. Methods: Changes in immunological markers were investigated in 82 patients with grass pollen-related allergic rhinoconjunctivitis who received active or placebo tablets sublingually once a day for four months. An allergen challenge with grass pollen was performed in the Vienna Challenge Chamber (VCC) at baseline, after 1 week, and after 1, 2 and 4 months of treatment. Blood samples were collected before treatment and after 2 and 4 treatment months for assessment of basophil activation (based on CD203c expression) and T cell responses (looking at proliferation, pheno-type, cytokine production and gene expression). Results: SLIT with a 5-grass-pollen tablet led to significant improvement (versus placebo) of 29.8% for the mean average rhinoconjunctivitis total symptom score (ARTSS) at end point. Clinical responders were defined as the 25% of patients with the highest relative improvement in symptom score from baseline, corresponding to at least a 48.9% decrease of ARTSS after treatment. No changes in basophil activation and T-cell proliferation were noticed for active and placebo groups in response to either the extract, Dac g 1 or Dac g 5 allergens, during treatment. Higher expression of Treg markers (eg Foxp 3) and lower expression of molecules associated with a Th1/Th2 profile were observed during treatment for both active and placebo groups. PMBCs from patients exposed to active treatment (versus placebo) displayed a lower production of TNF-alpha and a higher expression of IFN-gamma, with no differences between responders and non responders. All patients with a high symptom score before treatment responded to SLIT. However, neither basophil activation nor levels of T cell proliferation prior to treatment were predictive of efficacy. Conclusion: Basophil activation and T cell responses measured in the blood are not predictive of clinical responses induced by SLIT. Our results do not preclude that changes in cellular responses monitored in target respiratory mucosae can account for SLIT efficacy.
Heterogeneity of antibody responses among clinical responders following grass pollen sublingual immunotherapy; Background: Biomarkers of clinical efficacy are of major interest to monitor patients under specific sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT). To identify such surrogates, we investigated seric and mucosal antibody responses in the context of a randomised, double-blind placebo-controlled study conducted in an allergen challenge chamber. Methods: Changes in titres and affinity of allergen-specific IgE, IgG1-4, IgM and IgA were monitored in serum and nasal secretions in a cohort of 82 grass pollen allergic patients receiving once daily a sublingual 300IR grass pollen tablet or a placebo for 4 months. Average rhinoconjunctivitis total symptom score (ARTSS) was evaluated before and after 1 week, 1, 2 and 4 months of treatment, during allergen challenges in a pollen chamber. Results: A significant clinical response was observed in the group receiving the active treatment. The latter was documented in patients exhibiting distinct patterns of IgE sensitization (i.e. narrow, intermediate, broad) against Phl p 1 to 12 allergens. No neosensitization to grass pollen allergens was observed in the course of SLIT. Responders were defined as the 25% of patients with the highest relative improvement in symptom score from baseline, corresponding to at least a 48.9% decrease of ARTSS after treatment. Comparing antibody responses from patients belonging to each of the four following groups: Placebo responders/Placebo non responders/Active responders/Active non responders, we could establish that (i) Placebo responders exhibit clear grass pollen-specific antibody responses in nasal mucosa and (ii) Active responders are heterogeneous, encompassing both 'immunoreactive' patients with strong grass pollen-specific IgG, IgE and IgG4 responses (possibly blocking antibodies) induced during SLIT, as well as 'non immunoreactive' responders with no detectable immune responses distinguishing them from patients receiving placebo. Importantly, patients with high symptoms scores at inclusion were all improved under SLIT, although specific IgE levels prior to treatment were not predictive. Conclusion: SLIT with a grass pollen extract is similarly efficacious in patients exhibiting sensitization to single or multiple grass pollen allergens. Responders include both patients with strong seric allergen-specific antibody responses or lacking such responses. The latter observation suggests that additional immune mechanisms distinct from blocking antibodies are involved in SLIT efficacy.

There were benefits in having a group of 20 children all starting treatment at the same time and from the same area of the country. The pollen counts were obtained to compare symptom scoring with them and demonstrated that those patients with previously unmanaged SAR had much better control. Patients also utilised their questionnaires to comment on other family members' symptoms being present when theirs were not, contrary to their normal seasonal history. Persistence of specific grass pollen immunotherapies are similar to those observed in other long-term treatment regimens; Background: Specific immunotherapy (SIT) is a valid treatment option for moderateto-severe seasonal allergic rhinoconjunctivitis (SAR) caused by grass pollen. However, there are few data on persistence with long-term SIT regimens. Methods: Individual prescriptions/refill as a proxy for persistence (i.e. defined as the length of time during which the patient continues to be engaged with the prescribed dosing regimen) for three different SIT modalities (subcutaneous immunotherapy immunotherapy (SCIT) with natural allergens, SCIT with modified allergens (allergoids) and sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) with natural pollen extract solutions) were retrospectively tracked over 3 years (2005, 2006 and 2007) in a representative database of patients in Germany (INSIGHT Health). We determined whether SIT-naive patients receiving their first immunotherapy prescription in 2005 had renewed it for the same product group in 2006 and again in 2007. Results: A total of 1410 patients started SIT in 2005 with 112, 695 and 602 for natural extract SLIT, natural extract SCIT and allergoid SCIT, respectively). The distribution of the patients across the three groups reflects the documented market shares for these three SIT modalities in Germany. In 2006, the prescription renewal rates were 71%, 55% and 59%, respectively. In 2007, the rates (relative to 2005) were 51%, 34% and 39%. There were no significant differences between natural extract SCIT and allergoid SCIT (P = 0.1665 in 2006 and P = 0.0605 in 2007, in a chi-squared test) in terms of renewal. Prescription renewal rates for natural extract SLIT were significantly higher than those for natural extract SCIT (P = 0.0015 for 2006 and P = 0.0003 for 2007) and allergoid SCIT (P = 0.0152 for 2006 and P = 0.0111 for 2007). These findings confirm the issue of non-persistence with therapy in other chronic diseases in which non persistence at 6 months after start of therapy is as high as 50%. Conclusion: In a representative, German prescription database, all grass pollen SCIT and SLIT modalities displayed similar long-term prescription renewal rates to those observed in other chronic therapeutic regimens (diabetes, cardiovascular disease and acquired immunodeficiency syndrome, for example). Furthermore, our prescription renewal rate data counter the preconceived notion that SCIT (with injection in a medical environment) necessarily results in better overall persistence than SLIT (usually administered at home).
A role for phenology to appraise the really causative species in grass pollinosis; Background: Grass pollen is a worlwide cause of respiratory allergy throughout the world. Patients experience symptoms only when the pollen grains to which they are allergic are in the air and the level of symptoms is generally related to the pollen count. Identifying the causative grass species is essential when allergy is treated with specific immunotherapy (SIT). In fact, the allergen extract for SIT should contain the really responsible botanical species. Methods: We performed a phenological study to assess the flowering of different grass species. The following grasses were sampled: Black grass, Sweet vernal grass, Common wild oat, Barren brome, Cocksfoot, Tall fescue, Yorkshire fog, Perennial ryegrass, Timothy, Bulbous meadow-grass, Kentucky bluegrass (Pooideae), Bermuda grass (Chloridoideae). Ten areas in northern, central, and southern Italy, were chosen, with a total number of 50 stations. The recognition of the phenological flowering phase was performed using an electronmicroscopy based method for the detection of stamens spreading and release of pollen grains. The period of grass pollination was established according to the Italian official pollen calendars. Results: Evident differences were found between grass pollen counts and full flowering of the grass species assessed by phenology, with pollen peaks due only to some species and a relevant pollen load for various species also out of the peak periods. In particular, important Pooideae such as timothy are not present during the pollen peak in the north and centre of Italy and the same occurs with Bermuda grass over the entire territory. Conclusion: The clinical outcome of SIT is strictly dependent on the administration of an allergen extract fitting with patient's IgE sensitization. Concerning grasses, the use of a mixture seems to better reflect the natural exposure of the Italian population, and has the potential to provide a more complete interaction with the immunologic profile of grass sensitized patients.

The clinical development of specific immunotherapies: Specific methodological issues and clinical interpretation of results; Background: Historically, the safety and efficacy of specific immunotherapy (SIT) has been demonstrated in (mainly small-scale) studies and confirmed in meta-analyses. However, the inherent sources of heterogeneity (patient selection outside the pollen season, pollen count variations, long evaluation periods) observed in recent, large-scale studies of sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) tablets mean that highly susceptible patients may not exhibit uniformly a sufficient level of symptoms during the study period to assess the efficacy of SIT. Methods: We performed randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multinational clinical trials of a 300IR pre- and co-seasonally administered 5-grass pollen SLIT tablet in adults and children with allergic rhinitis. The primary efficacy criterion was the mean average rhinoconjunctivitis total symptom score (ARTSS) over the pollen season, during which daily grass pollen counts were measured locally. To evaluate the potential relationship between disease severity and the treatment effect, investigating centres were divided in tiertiles according to their mean placebo group ARTSS. Results: Pre-seasonal inclusion of patients on the basis of retrospectively severe symptoms in the previous pollen season did not produce such a severely affected population in the study season. The apparent treatment effect of SLIT tablet was partially masked by the highly variable severity of symptoms during the whole pollen season (mean ARTSS in the adult placebo group: 4.93 ± 3.229). For the adult trial, the mean active versus placebo ARTSSs and the relative difference versus placebo (%) were 15%, 26% and 37% for the low, moderate- and high-disease severity tiertiles, respectively. In the paediatric trial, these values were 10%, 33% and 34%, respectively. Linear regression of individual daily RTSS scores and pollen counts in active and placebo groups also showed that the more severe the disease, the greater the treatment effect of SLIT tablet. Conclusion: Inherent sources of heterogeneity must be taken into account when interpreting the results of natural-exposure immunotherapy trials but none obscured the statistically significant treatment effect of SLIT. In a subgroup analysis, SLIT tablets' beneficial effect increased with disease severity.

Long-lasting clinical efficacy of allergen specific immunotherapy in adults; Background: Many controlled studies have demonstrated that allergen immunotherapy is the unique specific and effective treatment of allergic rhinitis (AR) and/or asthma. However, only limited knowledge exists about the long-term clinical efficacy of this therapy. Aim: This study was designed as retrospective controlled observational trial. Patients with AR and/or asthma treated with conventional immunotherapy between 1992 and 2000 years and those completing the previous SIT at least 5 years ago were included into the study. The control group composed of patients not receiving SIT during the same period. The two groups were well matched in terms of age, onset of disease and severity, and allergen sensitivity. Patients who had eligible medical records were invited for assessment in 2007 in terms of their symptoms, drug intake, skin test and non-specific bronchial reactivity since the end of the previous SIT in 2000. SIT and control groups were comparatively evaluated regarding at the beginning (T0), end of the SIT (T1) and the current status (T2). Results: Out of 154 patients, 30 SIT (F/M: 21/9, mean age: 30 ± 7.4 years) and 26 control group (F/M: 19/7, mean age: 31.3 ± 7.2 years) provided inclusion criteria. They were re-evaluated for a time period (mean 12.1 ± 2.5 years) including duration of SIT (4.5 ± 0.9 years) after T0 time point. Rhinitis, asthma and medication scores were significantly reduced at T2 compared to T0 and T1 (P = 0.000). Duration of SIT for a longer periods was found to be only independent factor affecting good clinical response. Twenty-two (39.2%) of a total 56 patients developed new sensitizations according to skin prick tests regardless of the groups (P = 0.278). However, the rate of 'symptomatic sensitization' among them was significantly higher in the control group (23.1%) than in the SIT group (3.3%) (P = 0.041). There was a significant decrease in skin test reactivity against grass pollen antigens, and the positivity of methacholine bronchial challenge test between T0 and T2 in the SIT group (P = 0.016). No significant change was observed in lung function parameters as well as specific and total IgE levels. Conclusion: Our study indicates that there is still an important clinical benefit average 7 years after discontinuation of SIT in adults. A striking finding of this study was not prevented development of new sensitization by the SIT. Neverthless, it seems that SIT may play a suppressive role in the onset of overt clinical symptoms.

The practice, safety and efficacy of immunotherapy in East Midlands; Background: Immunotherapy is known to be highly effective and to modify the natural history of allergic rhinitis and offer potential for long term disease remission. The results of a dose-finding phase IIb/III clinical trial of Oralair Birch were positive, with the primary endpoint met by all three tested doses. A confirmatory phase III trial was planned for 2011. Oralair Birch is a very promising treatment option for patients with birch pollen allergic rhinitis. © Thomson Reuters (Scientific) Ltd.

▼Grazax for hay fever - What's new?; In 2008, we reviewed Grazax, a sublingual tablet containing standardised allergen extract of grass pollen.1 At the time, this product was licensed for the treatment of adults with proven grass-pollen-induced rhinitis and conjunctivitis (hay fever). However, we were not convinced that the effect on rhinoconjunctivitis symptom scores in published trials was clinically relevant. Does specific immunotherapy act on innate immunity?; Specific immunotherapy (SIT), whether it be subcutaneous or sublingual, relies upon several intricate antigen-specific immune mechanisms, including the modulation of CD4+ T cell responses (stimulation of Th1 and T Reg responses), as well as the induction of anti-inflammatory "blocking" antibodies (IgG4 or IgA). The impact of SIT on innate immunity (i. E., antigen-independent) has yet to be investigated, but may encompass a direct effect on epithelial cells, dendritic cells (DCs), and/or mast cells and basophils. Mucous epithelial cells are the first to come in contact with allergen, and their response to this stimulus differs between allergic and non-allergic individuals. SIT has been reported to modulate the function of plasmacytoid DCs in the peripheral blood (with induction of IFNα secretion following stimulation with a TLR9 ligand), and the question is raised as to whether SIT can elicit a "tolerogenic" phenotype in DCs. With this in view, we are currently engaged in a proteomic study aiming to identify potential molecular markers of regulatory DCs. SIT appears to have an effect on the activation of tissue mast cells and circulating basophils (probably via regulation of activation signals). Nonetheless, our recent SLIT study in grass pollen allergic patients dœs not confirm a correlation between clinical efficacy and a decrease in circulating basophil activation. © 2010 Elsevier Masson SAS. All rights reserved.

Molecular variability of group 1 and 5 grass pollen allergens between Pooideae species: Implications for immunotherapy; Background Differences between major allergens from distinct grass species remain to be investigated, both in terms of structure and antigenicity. Methods Group 1 and 5 allergens purified from five common Pooideae species were analysed by mass spectrometry (MS). Major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class II-restricted T cell epitopes were identified using predictive algorithms and human leucocyte antigen (HLA)-binding assays. CD4+ T cell reactivity and IgE binding were assessed based on the induction of CD154 expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells and using competitive ELISA assays, respectively. Results MS analysis of group 5 pollen allergens reveals considerable intra- and inter-species variability in amino acid sequence, with 30-50 predominant isoforms found for each species. Differences in the amino acid sequence as well as N- and O-glycosylation contribute to the variability of group 1 allergens, yielding 5-10 main isoforms, depending on the species. Out of 14 MHC class II-restricted T cell epitopes identified within group 1, only one is conserved among the five grass species. Significant differences in binding affinities for HLA-DR molecules result in variable CD4+ T cell recognition of group 1 and 5 allergens purified from the various species. Up to 38% and 85% of patients exhibit seric IgE responses to species-restricted (or semi-restricted) epitopes associated with group 1 or 5 allergens, respectively. Conclusion Major pollen allergens from distinct grass species bear both shared and species-restricted T and B cell immune epitopes. When compared with single extracts, a five grass pollen extract is thus more suitable for specific immunotherapy, as it contains a broader repertoire of the IgE epitopes to which patients are sensitized. © 2009 Blackwell Publishing Ltd.
Allergen immunotherapy; Specific immunotherapy (SIT) involves the administration of allergen extracts to achieve clinical tolerance of those allergens that cause symptoms in patients with allergic conditions. Immunotherapy is effective in patients with mild forms of allergic disease and also in those who do not respond well to standard drug therapy. Most SIT is given by means of injection, but there is increasing interest in performing SIT through the sublingual route. SIT remains the treatment of choice for patients with systemic allergic reactions to wasp and bee stings and should be considered as an option in patients with allergic rhinitis, asthma, or both. SIT can modify the course of allergic disease by reducing the risk of new allergic sensitizations and inhibiting the development of clinical asthma in children treated for allergic rhinitis. The precise mechanisms responsible for the beneficial effects of SIT remain a matter of research and debate. An effect on regulatory T cells seems most probable and is associated with switching of allergen-specific B cells toward IgG4 production. Few direct comparisons of SIT and drug therapy have been made. Existing data suggest that the effects of SIT take longer to develop, but once established, SIT achieves long-lasting relief of allergic symptoms, whereas the benefits of drugs only last as long as they are continued. © 2010 American Academy of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology.

Identification of T-cell epitopes of Phl p 5a as a basic requirement for construction of hypoallergenic Mutants; RATIONALE: Recombinant Phl p 5a derivatives are promising candidates for an allergen cocktail for specific immunotherapy based on hypo-allergenic Timothy grass major allergens. An important prerequisite for construction of such mutants is identification of T-cell epitopes on Phl p 5a. METHODS: T-cell lines were raised from PBMC of grass pollen allergic subjects with natural or recombinant Phl p 5a. T-cell epitopes were analyzed with synthetic dodeca peptides spanning the whole sequence of 288 amino acids of rPhl p 5a overlapping by 3 residues. T-cell reactivity was measured by proliferation assays using 3H-Thymidine. RESULTS: Results from 30 TCL of 16 different grass pollen allergics are included. Two dominant regions of T-cell reactivity are found in the N-ter-minal part of Phl p 5a at positions 13-27 and 40-54. Four further dominant regions are located in the C-terminal half of the molecule at positions 160174, 172-186, 196-228 and 229-252. Further peptides with lower frequencies of T-cell reactivity were found between positions 55-162. The T-cell reactivity of a mutant with deletions at positions 94-113 and 175-190 coincides with these findings. CONCLUSIONS: Five regions of frequent T-cell reactivity could be determined on Phl p 5a, together with one region with T-cell reactivity of lower frequency and 5 - 6 regions with no T-cell reactivity. The latter segments of the molecule are those where genetic engineering might produce promising mutants with a changed conformation and reduced IgE-reactivity.

Clinical parameters to evaluate the efficacy of allergen-specific immunotherapy in allergic rhinoconjunctivitis. Calculation of "well days" as an adjunct concept; Efficacy monitoring of immunotherapy (IT) is performed to adjust the therapy according to the patients reactions, to collect data for scientific studies and to evaluate the efficacy of IT. A decrease of allergy symptoms and of drug use are the main efficacy parameters obtained by using the symptom-medication-score (SMS). For this, allergy diaries, skin tests and nasal provocation testing are most suitable. During the period of documentation pollen exposition should be monitored with Burkhard traps. In cytologic measures specific cell activation markers and specific lymphokine-profiles can be evaluated. For the reason of their expense, those methods are restricted to scientific investigations and only rarely for routine diagnostics. Numerous clinical trials have investigated the efficacy and safety of sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) using symptom- and medication-scores. The results suggest that high allergen doses are necessary to achieve adequate efficacy. An alternative approach to assess the outcome of allergen-specific immunotherapy was investigated by a new high-dose sublingual 6-grass pollen preparation. This sublingual immunotherapy significantly improved the symptom-medication-score (SMS) in a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial by counting "well days" (days without intake of any rescue medication and a reduction of the symptom-score) during the grass pollen season. This post-hoc analysis showed that SLIT for 1.5 years resulted in a significantly higher number of "well days" than with placebo. These results reflect the high improvement in symptom-medication-score. "Well days" can therefore be regarded as a further variable to measure efficacy of allergen-specific immunotherapy. © 2010 Dustri-Verlag Dr. Karl Feistle.

Omalizumab represents an important clinical advance in the management of allergic diseases and can be considered to be safe in children. © 2009 John Wiley & Sons A/S.

Component Resolved Diagnosis (CRD): In-vitro definition of allergic patient's profile; Molecular characterization of IgE reactivity of specific individual components of allergenic extracts is now possible due to the technology of recombinant allergens derived from studies of molecular biology of allergic pathology. The identification of the immunoreactivity to single allergenic components in allergic individuals allows to specifically define her/his allergic profile and obtain the so-termed Component Resolved Diagnosis (CRD). Molecular allergens can be classified into those that induce the respiratory allergic reactivity and those that identify the food-related allergic pathology. It is also essential to identify those molecular allergens whose immunoreactivity is able to connect the two clinical conditions: respiratory symptoms and food allergic symptoms. Proteins intervening in the defence system of plants belonging to the group of Pathogenesis-Related proteins (PR-10) are the best characterized molecules in the recent years. Within the Pr-10 group of allergens, Bet v 1, the major allergen from birch pollen, is responsible not only for allergic respiratory reactions but also for food allergic reactions (Oral Allergy Syndrome - SOA). The family of profiline is another well characterized group of molecular allergens, which includes Bet v 2 (birch profiline), whose allergic immunoreactivity is also responsible for more than one allergic symptom. Interestingly, response to immunotherapy can be predicted from immunoreactivity. For instance, in the case of IgE reactivity to grass pollen, subjects positive to Phl p 1 (protein "Beta-Expansin") and Phl p 5 (ribonuclease) and negative to Phl p 7 (PR-10 of grass and cross-reactive with Bet v1) and to Phl p 12 (profiline of grass and crossreactive with Bet v 2) seem to respond better to the vaccine. Moreover, the availability of the first recombinant Phl p 5 vaccines suggests to characterize properly the IgE response to this molecular antigen. As for the sensitisation to flour food, whose vegetal origin is still belonging to the grasses we should consider the syndrome of Wheat-Dependent Exercise-induced Anaphylaxis (WDEIA) that would be defined by allergic immunoreactivity to the omega-5 gliadin molecule. Another series of molecules that connect vegetal world both of pollen and of food origin are the Lipid Transfer Protein, whose allergenic reactivity would also be responsible for severe symptoms. In conclusion, understanding the relationship between allergic symptoms and the profile of immunoreactivity to the molecular components of an allergen in each individual is therefore crucial.
Treatment with the SQ-standardised grass allergy immunotherapy tablet in children above and below the age of 10 - Efficacy, safety and immunological response; Purpose: Treatment with the SQ-standardised grass allergen immunotherapy tablet (AIT), GRAZAX® (Phleum pratense 75,000 SQ-T/2,800 BAU, ALK, Denmark), is efficacious and well-tolerated in grass allergic patients. Methods: Of 253 children aged 5-16 years with grass allergy were randomised 1:1 to receive grass AIT or placebo prior to and during the grass pollen season 2007. Results: Analysis of the difference between active and placebo for each age group showed a slightly higher relative difference in symptom score for the younger children compared with the older, 26% versus 19%. The percentages of adverse events assessed as moderate or severe in the active group were similar for the two age groups. For both active and placebo, the overall number of adverse events was higher in the younger group than in the group of older children. The immunological response (IgE, IgG4 and IgE-blocking factor) was similar for the two age groups. There was a tendency for the younger group towards an increased response in IgE-blocking factor at the onset of the grass pollen season, both in the active and the placebo group. Conclusions: The phase III trial, investigating the SQ-standardised grass AIT, demonstrated once-daily administration to be clinically efficacious and well-tolerated in children between 5 and 16 years. Comparison of two age groups revealed similar efficacy and tolerability after treatment with grass AIT independent of age.

Sustained, disease-modifying effect of grass allergy tablet immunotherapy 1 year after a 3-year treatment period; Background: The sustained efficacy with the SQ-standardised grass allergy immunotherapy tablet (AIT), Grazax® (Phleum pratense 75,000 SQ-T, ALK-Abello, Denmark), 1 year after a 3-year treatment period, was investigated in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase III trial. Participants were adults with a history of moderate to severe grass pollen induced rhinoconjunctivitis inadequately controlled by symptomatic medications. Methods: The full analysis set included 283 participants (157 AIT, 126 placebo). All participants had free access to symptomatic medications during the grass pollen season. Primary and key secondary efficacy endpoints were rhinoconjunctivitis symptom and medication scores, quality of life, and percentages of symptom and medication free days. Immunological endpoints included specific IgG4 and IgE-blocking factor. Safety was assessed by adverse events. Results: 1 year after treatment, the grass AIT group showed a 26% reduction in mean rhinoconjunctivitis symptom scores (P < 0.001) and a 29% reduction in medication scores (P = 0.022) when compared with placebo. The corresponding median reductions were 31% and 52%. This level of efficacy was similar to the efficacy during treatment. The mean difference in percentages of symptom and medication free days during the entire season was 27% (P= 0.038) (median difference 49%) in favour of AIT. The grass AIT group also reported better rhinoconjunctivitis quality of life (P= 0.004). No safety issues were identified. Conclusion: Significant and clinically relevant efficacy of grass AIT was sustained 1 year after a 3-year treatment period. This is the first time evidence of disease modification by sublingual tablet immunotherapy has been demonstrated in a large-scale, randomised, placebo-controlled trial.
Rationale for five-grass pollen vaccine; Grass pollen. allergic patients are naturally exposed and sensitized to multiple pollens from various Pooideae species. The question arises as to whether such patients should be desensitized with extracts based on a single pollen or a pollen mixture. Neither conventional diagnosis based on IgE reactivity nor pollen counts enable the identification of which grass species are involved in patient sensitization. Significant cross-immunogenicity is observed between allergens from Pooideae pollens due to their conserved amino acid sequences (e.g. > 90% for group 1, 55-80% for group 5, 30-60% for other allergens, including minor allergens). Nevertheless, pollen allergens also contain species-specific T or B cell epitopes, and there is evidence that at least 50% of allergic patients are sensitized to such distinct epitopes. In addition, substantial quantitative differences exist in the allergen (e.g. group 1, 2/3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 13) content of pollens obtained from distinct grass species. In this context, we recommend a vaccine consisting of a combination of pollens from five common and well characterized Pooideae including Anthoxanthum odoratum, Dactylis glomerata, Lolium perenne, Phleum pratense and Poa pratensis for desensitization purposes. This 5-grass mixture is recommended because, (i) it has been validated, in terms of safety and efficacy, by established clinical practice
Extensive ige cross-reactivity towards the pooideae grasses substantiated for a large number of grass-pollen-sensitized subjects; Background: Allergy to taxonomically related species is a common phenomenon caused by the same immunological receptor cross-reacting to homologous allergens from different species. Knowledge of patterns of cross-reactivity is crucial for the selection of optimal products for diagnosis and for specific immunotherapy. The objective of this study was to investigate patterns of serum IgE cross-reactivity towards pollens from various grass species. Methods: With grass group 1 allergens as the representative group, amino acid sequence alignment, structural modelling and comparison of 3D surface characteristics were performed to exemplify the molecular basis of IgE cross-reactivity. IgE binding to extracts from ten different grass species was determined (total number of data pairs >19,000), and IgE inhibition experiments using Phleum pratense were performed. Results: Analysis of surface topography for group 1 grass allergens demonstrated ample space for IgE binding epitopes in surface areas conserved among Pooideae grasses. Significant correlation was observed between the serum IgE response to P. pratense extract and extracts from the other Pooideae grasses analyzed. P. pratense extract was demonstrated to inhibit the binding of IgE to the allergens in all of the extracts included in the investigation, indicating patient IgE to be primarily directed towards common epitopes. Conclusion: Extensive IgE cross-reactivity was observed towards the allergens of the Pooideae grasses, meaning that the immune system does not appear to distinguish based on the IgE level between the different species of this subfamily. The data suggest equal effect upon use of any of the Pooideae species for diagnostic as well as therapeutic purposes. © 2009 S. Karger AG, Basel.

The SQ-standardized grass allergy immunotherapy tabletis well tolerated over 3 years of treatment; Introduction: Traditionally, allergen-specific immunotherapy has been administered via subcutaneous injections or sublingual drops. Recently, a new formulation administered sublingually, allergy immunotherapy tablets (AIT), has emerged. Many large double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trials have demonstrated AIT to be well tolerated and efficacious in reducing rhinoconjunctivitis symptoms and the use of rescue medications. We investigated the nature, severity and duration of the most common adverse events (AEs) associated with treatment with an SQ-standardized grass AIT (Phleum pratense, 75,000 SQ-T/2,800 BAU, ALK, Denmark) during a trial conducted over a 3 year period. Methods: Subjects with grass-allergy (n=634) were enrolled in a double-blind, placebo-controlled, multinational trial, of which 351 continued in a 2-year extension. Approval was obtained from the local IRBs and written informed consent obtained from all subjects. Subjects were randomized 1:1 to grass AIT or placebo. All AEs were collected and rated as mild, moderate or severe. AEs were assessed as treatment-emergent if the start date was on or after the date of the first tablet intake. Reactions occurring for a limited period of time each day on consecutive days were reported as one event. Results: The most frequent AEs after grass AIT were oral pruritus (164 subjects, 191 events), mouth edema (65 subjects, 70 events), ear pruritus (41 subjects, 42 events) and throat irritation (34 subjects, 37 events). The majority of these AEs were mild (84%) or moderate (13%) and transient of nature. There was a sharp decrease in the percentage of subjects reporting these AEs within the first weeks ofthe trial (figure). Approximately 10% continued to have oral itching during the entire trial, typically lasting 10 minutes after tablet administration. Withdrawal due to these local AEs was low (n=6, 1%). Conclusions: The most frequent AEs after grass AIT were local reactions affecting the mucosal membranes in mouth, ear and throat. The majority of AEs were mild and generally subsided shortly after treatment initiation, indicating development of tolerance. A small proportion of the subjects experienced local AEs daily upon tablet administration. However, the rate of withdrawals due to local AEs was low, indicating that grass AIT was well tolerated and these side effects were acceptable to most patients. (Figure Presented).
Cross-reactivity between pollen allergens from common Pooideae grasses and rye; In Germany ,specific pollen extracts are currently used for immunotherapy of rye (Secale cereale) allergy. Diagnosis and management of allergic rhinitis; • Objective: To provide an overview of the approach to diagnosis and management of allergic rhinitis. • Methods: Review of the literature. • Results: Allergic rhinitis affects 20% to 40% of the U.S. population and has a significant impact on patients, their families, and society. The diagnosis can often be ascertained from a history that points to a specific, often seasonal or environmental, trigger. Treatment is often begun without the aid of any testing and based on a diagnosis made on history and physical examination alone. The mainstays of first-line treatment are nonsedating oral antihistamines, nasal corticosteroids, and nasal antihistamine sprays. As an adjunct, mast cell stabilizing antihistamine eye drops may be used. First-line pharmacotherapy should be based on the nature and severity of the patient's symptoms. Allergy testing should be considered when a patient's symptoms are not controlled by routine medical therapies. • Conclusion: Allergy is a significant burden to society. A symptom-based approach to the pharmacologic treatment of allergic rhinitis will yield the most satisfactory control of the patient's major symptoms.
The future of sublingual immunotherapy.; Sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) is currently the most prescribed form of allergen immunotherapy in many European countries. Its use has been accepted in the international consensus publications, and recently also the scepticism of USA scientists is attenuated. Still, this treatment may be improved, and the possible developments consist of modification of the materials, use of adjuvants and use of recombinant allergens. Moreover, new applications of SLIT, such as food allergy, seem promising. Concerning materials, the future form of SLIT is likely to be represented by tablets, which were already tested for efficacy and safety with grass pollen extracts, and are likely to increase the convenience for the patient by the use of no-updosing schedule. Adjuvants fitting with the characteristics of SLIT seem to be CpG oligodeoxynucleotides (CpG), able to interact with the Toll-like receptor 9 (TLR9) whose activation induces a Th1-like pattern of cytokine release, combination of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3 plus dexamethasone (VitD3-Dex), and Lactobacillus plantarum. The approach with recombinant allergens, named component-resolved diagnosis, offers the possibility to tailor immunotherapy, which was found to be effective in two randomized trials of subcutaneous SIT (16-17), while studies with SLIT are not yet available. Regarding food allergy, an important controlled study demonstrated that SLIT with hazelnut is able to increase patients tolerance over possible reactions from inadvertent assumption of the culprit food, and warrants for further trials with other foods.

The main mechanism of action is the interaction with dendritic cells of the oral mucosa and the subsequent tolerance induced in T cells. © 2009 Informa UK Ltd All rights reserved.
Efficacy of grass pollen sublingual immunotherapy for three consecutive seasons and after cessation of treatment: The ECRIT study; Background: Data supporting a carry-over effect with sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) are scarce. This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study evaluated the efficacy, carry-over effect and safety of grass pollen SLIT using co-seasonal treatment. Methods: Patients (7.9-64.7 years) with grass pollen allergy received ultra-rush titration with increasing doses (30, 90, 150 and 300 IR) of a 5-grass pollen mixture every 20 min at the start of the pollen seasons, followed by 300 IR daily until the end of the pollen seasons. A baseline season (no SLIT) was followed by three consecutive treatment seasons and one follow-up season. Symptoms, medication and adverse events were documented and specific immunoglobulin (Ig)E and IgG4 measured. Results: Data were analysed for 183 of the 213 randomized patients. Mean treatment duration varied between seasons (81.8-92.7 days). Combined scores (symptoms and medication) improved progressively across treatment seasons (up to 44.7% improvement for SLIT compared with baseline) and fluctuated between -11.3% and -14.8% for placebo (P < 0.05). Similar changes were observed for symptom scores, with a successive decrease of 39.7% (SLIT) and fluctuations between +13.6% and -1.51% for placebo (P < 0.05). Combined score (P = 0.0508) and symptom score improvements (P = 0.0144) with SLIT continued during follow up. Increases in specific IgG4 observed in the first season were sustained for SLIT vs placebo throughout treatment (P = 0.0001). Titration and daily SLIT were well tolerated. No serious systemic or anaphylactic reactions were reported. Conclusions: Seasonal SLIT with ultra-rush titration is well tolerated and effective from the first treatment season onwards. These data indicate a carry-over effect of seasonal SLIT. © 2008 The Authors.
Slowing progression along the allergic disease continuum: Quo vadit immunotherapy?; There is emerging evidence that rhinitis frequently precedes the onset of asthmatic symptoms. The frequent association of rhinitis and asthma has led to the concept that these conditions are likely manifestations of the same disease. This hypothesis has important implications for both the diagnosis and the management of these common conditions. Unfortunately, there is little known regarding the risk factors responsible for the progression of rhinitis to asthma. The current treatment options can control symptoms but do not prevent or cure the disease. However, there is recent data supporting the notion that it is possible to prevent new asthma cases by modifying the immune response and clinical outcome with allergen immunotherapy. This review article evaluates the impact of rhinitis on the development of asthma, examines putative predictors for the progression of rhinitis to asthma, and reviews recent, promising literature suggesting that early treatment of allergic individuals with immunotherapy may aid in asthma prevention. © 2009 Mary Ann Liebert, Inc.

Mass spectrometric investigation of molecular variability of grass pollen group 1 allergens; Natural grass pollen allergens exhibit a wide variety of isoforms. Precise characterization of such microheterogeneity is essential to improve diagnosis and design appropriate immunotherapies. Moreover, standardization of allergen vaccine production is a prerequisite for product safety and efficiency. Both qualitative and quantitative analytical methods are thus required to monitor and control the huge natural variability of pollens, as well as final product quality. A proteomic approach has been set up to investigate in depth the structural variability of five group 1 allergens originating from distinct grass species (Ant o 1, Dac g 1, Lol p 1, Phl p 1, and Poa p 1). Whereas group 1 is the most conserved grass pollen allergen, great variations were shown between the various isoforms found in these five species using mass spectrometry, with many amino acid exchanges, as well as variations in proline hydroxylation level and in main N-glycan motifs. The presence of O-linked pentose residues was also demonstrated, with up to three consecutive units on the first hydroxyproline of Ant o 1. In addition, species-specific peptides were identified that might be used for product authentication or individual allergen quantification. Lastly, natural or process-induced modifications (deamidation, oxidation, glycation) were evidenced, which might constitute useful indicators of product degradation. © 2009 American Chemical Society.

Safety of sublingual grass pollen immunotherapy after anaphylaxis; Aim: To demonstrate that sublingual immunotherapy is a safe treatment option in patients who have previously suffered anaphylaxis when undergoing subcutaneous grass pollen immunotherapy. Allergen-specific immunotherapy in allergic rhinitis and asthma. Mechanisms and proof of efficacy; Appeared at the beginning of the 20th century, allergen-specific immunotherapy (SIT) has long been used in allergic rhinitis and asthma without any knowledge of its mechanisms of action or any tangible proof of its efficacy. However, from the beginning of the era of evidence-based medicine, a number of placebo-controlled studies have been published and reached a sufficient number to assess the cellular events induced by SIT and allow meta-analysis to provide guidelines based on proofs. Controlled studies and meta-analysis concerned not only subcutaneous immunotherapy but also the sublingual route, demonstrating an effect of SIT on symptoms and medication use. Most recently sublingual tablets were proposed in allergic rhinitis. This paper reviews the mechanisms of SIT, the evidence of efficacy of SIT from the injective to the sublingual route and reminds the current guidelines. © 2009 Elsevier Ltd. All rights reserved.
Sublingual immunotherapy for children: Are we there yet?. Defining its role in clinical practice; Immunotherapy in various forms has been used to treat allergic disorders since the early 19th century. Subcutaneous immunotherapy is now well established for the treatment of insect anaphylaxis and allergic rhinitis. The route of administration and possibility of severe adverse reactions to subcutaneous immunotherapy make sublingual immunotherapy an appealing alternative, especially for the paediatric patient. This form of immunotherapy has been increasingly used in Europe, and over the past decade several meta analyses have attempted to provide evidence for its efficacy in the treatment of seasonal and perennial allergic rhinitis and in asthma, both in the adult and paediatric population. Several trials have also shown a potential immunomodulatory effect of sublingual immunotherapy, with evidence of a reduction in the progression from allergic rhinitis to asthma and reduced new aeroallergen sensitisation. This review will give an overview of the current evidence for sublingual immunotherapy in the paediatric population. Crown Copyright © 2009.
Molecular variability of Group 1 and 5 pollen allergens between Pooideae grass species: Implications for immunotherapy; Background: Grass pollen allergic patients are concomitantly exposed and sensitized to pollen allergens originating from multiple Pooideae species. Despite a high aminoacid sequence homology, qualitative differences between major allergens from distinct grass species remain to be investigated, both in terms of structure and antigenicity. Methods: Group 1 and group 5 allergens purified by hydrophobic interaction chromatography from each of Anthoxanthum odoratum, Dactylis glomerata, Lolium perenne, Phleum pratense and Poa pratensis pollens were analysed by mass spectrometry. MHC class II restricted T cell epitopes were identified within group 1 allergens using predictive algorithms and in vitro HLA binding assays. T cell reactivity was analysed using purified group 1 and group 5 allergens based on the induction of CD154 expression in PBMCs, detected by cytofluorometry. IgE binding affinities to purified allergens were assessed in competitive Elisa assays using individual sera from 28 grass pollen allergic patients. Results: Mass spectrometry analysis of purified group 5 allergens obtained from five common Pooideae species revealed both considerable intra and inter species variability in amino acid sequence, with 20-50 predominant isoforms found for each species. Both amino acid sequence variants, but also glycoforms contribute to the variability of group 1 major allergens. Within group 1, up to fourteen potential MHC class II restricted T cell epitopes have been identified, out of which only one is conserved among the five grass species. Significant differences exist in the affinity of such species-specific T cell epitopes for common HLA-DR haplotypes. A substantial variability in CD4+ T cell recognition of group 1 and group 5 allergens from various species is confirmed for allergic patients. Up to 85% patients exhibit seric IgE responses to species-restricted (or semi-restricted) epitopes, associated with group 1 or group 5 allergens, whereas all of them have crossreactive IgEs against conserved epitopes. Conclusions: Due to considerable molecular variability between grass species, major pollen allergens bear both shared and species-restricted T and B cell epitopes. As a consequence, specific immunotherapy for grass pollen allergy should ideally be performed with a mixture of pollens from common Pooideae, in order to reflect natural exposure and sensitisation conditions, at a molecular and submolecular (i.e. epitopic) level.

Sustained, disease-modifying effect of grass allergen tablet immunotherapy 1 year after completion of treatment; Background: The sustained efficacy following withdrawal of ALK grass allergen immunotherapy tablet (AIT), Grazax (Phleum pratense 75,000 SQ-T/2,800 BAU, ALK-Abello, Hørsholm, Denmark) was investigated in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase III trial. Participants were followed for 1 year after completion of a 3-year period of daily treatment. Participants were adults with a clinical history of moderate to severe grass pollen allergy inadequately controlled by the use of symptomatic medication. Methods: The full analysis set included 283 participants (157 active, 126 placebo) who entered the follow-up investigation 1 year after completion of 3 years treatment. Efficacy endpoints comprised rhinoconjunctivitis symptom and medication scores, quality of life, and percentages of symptom and medication free days. Immunological endpoints included serum levels of grass pollen specific IgG4 and IgE-blocking factor. Safety was assessed by means of adverse events. Results: One year after completion of treatment the active group showed a 26% reduction in rhinoconjunctivitis symptom scores (P < 0.001) and a 29% reduction in medication scores (P < 0.02) when compared with placebo over the entire grass pollen season. The difference in percentages of symptom and medication free days during the entire season was 27% (P = 0.04) in favour of AIT. Participants in the active group also reported better rhinoconjunctivitis quality of life both during the entire grass pollen season and during the peak season. The IgE-binding activity of grass extracts was calculated by comparison with their corresponding reference extracts using EAST-inhibition assays. Results: The assays were dose-dependent, and the standard dose-response curves revealed a sigmoid shape when plotted on a semilogarithmic scale. The linear portion of the standard curve of group 1 was found in the range from 125 to 1000 ng/ml, with a regression coefficient of 0.999 and a detection limit of 31 ng/ml. For group 5, the range was 0.08 to 1.25 ng/ml, with a regression coefficient of 0.995 and a detection limit of 25 pg/ml. The inter-assay and intra-assay variation coefficients were in all cases <20%. The dose-response curves obtained with group 1 and group 5 purified allergens were parallel to those obtained with the pollen extracts. These allergens was measured in 19 L. perenne and 8 P. pretense pollen extracts, showing an average content of 10.6, 3.3, 17.4, and 3.2% for Lol p 1, Lol p 5, Phl p 1 and Phl p 5, respectively. Group 1 and group 5 grass allergen content showed a significant correlation with their IgE-binding activity. Conclusion: These sensitive and specific assays are helpful to determine group 1 and group 5 allergen content of grass pollen extracts intended for clinical use.
The novel acute adjuvant-free murine model of bronchial asthma induced by timothy pollen allergen; Background: The purpose of the study was to develop an acute mouse model of bronchial asthma (BA) based on timothy pollen allergen without adjuvant and to establish the immunological, cellular, morphological and functional airway features of this model.
